Kaiser (Neurergus kaiseri) larvae emerge from their protective jelly capsules after an incubation period that is heavily dependent on thermal conditions. When maintained at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the eggs typically hatch after a period of approximately 17.5 days [ab = approximately 17.5 days], though the natural range spans from two to three weeks. This incubation duration aligns with values documented for other members of the genus Salamandridae under similar thermal regimes. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larvae are notably small, with a mean length at birth of 1.494 cm [Lb = 1.494 cm], a measurement initially reported for the closely related Neurergus microspilotus. The larval period is a protracted phase of development; metamorphosis does not typically occur until roughly seven months  have elapsed since hatching, under the same constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. During this time, the exogenously feeding tadpoles grow substantially, and the transition to a terrestrial juvenile form is marked by a length at metamorphosis of 3.1 cm .

By the time metamorphic climax concludes, the recently metamorphosed juveniles have achieved a wet weight of approximately 1.5 g , a mass that reflects the considerable growth achieved during the aquatic larval stage. This body mass is consistent with the energetic demands of the morphological transformation, which includes tail resorption and limb development. Following the transition to a terrestrial lifestyle, juvenile Kaiser salamanders undergo a prolonged period of somatic growth before reaching reproductive maturity. The time since birth at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, is approximately 4 years [tp = approximately 4 years] when individuals are maintained at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This relatively late maturation is characteristic of slow-paced life histories observed in montane amphibian populations, where cooler temperatures constrain metabolic and developmental rates compared to lowland congeners.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is evident among mature individuals of this species. Adult females have a maximum snout-vent length (SVL) of 7.5 cm [Li = 7.5 cm], a value that represents the ultimate body size recorded for female Kaiser salamanders. In contrast, adult males reach a smaller ultimate body size, with a maximum SVL of 5.5 cm [Li = 5.5 cm]. This degree of female-biased size dimorphism is typical of many salamandrid species and is often attributed to fecundity selection, where larger body size in females permits the carriage of a greater number of eggs. The body mass of mature females is correspondingly higher than that of males, contributing to an overall pattern of sexual size dimorphism that is an important component of the species' life history strategy.

Reproductive output in this species is tied to the capacity of gravid females to produce a large clutch. Each female deposits between 50 and 100 eggs over the course of a single breeding season [Ri = between 50 and 100 eggs over the course of a single breeding season], reflecting a substantial energetic investment in offspring. Field observations indicate that females typically complete only a single reproductive bout per year [F_R_i = single reproductive bout per year], a frequency constrained by the necessity to accumulate sufficient energy reserves following the previous season's effort. At a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], this annual pattern results in a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 0.14 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 0.14 offspring per day], a low rate compared to species breeding in warmer, more productive habitats, but it is an adaptation to the stable, cool streams that constitute the salamander's native environment.

Lifespan estimates differ between the sexes, a pattern observed in various amphibian taxa. In captivity, the maximum recorded longevity for male Kaiser salamanders is 14 years [am = 14 years] when maintained at a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Female individuals have a slightly shorter maximum lifespan, documented at 12 years [am = 12 years] under identical thermal conditions, representing the oldest documented female individual. This discrepancy may be linked to the elevated metabolic and physiological costs associated with annual reproduction and egg production in females, which could accelerate the rate of physiological aging. These longevity values are notably high among urodeles of comparable body size and highlight the extended generational turnover that characterizes the life history of Neurergus kaiseri in its native habitat.
